chain.g: what is owed, a debt, a duty

ety.text: From Middle English dette, dett, borrowed from Old French dete (French dette), from Medieval Latin dēbita, from Latin dēbitum (“what is owed, a debt, a duty”), neuter of dēbitus, perfect passive participle of dēbeō (“to owe”), contraction of *dehibeō (“I have from”), from de (“from”) + habeō (“to have”). Doublet of debit. Displaced native Old English eofot. The unpronounced "b" in the modern English spelling is a Latinisation from the Latin etymon dēbitum.

senses.d: An action, state of mind, or object one has an obligation to perform for another, adopt toward another, or give to another.
ex: This long debt of confidence, due from me to him, whose bane and ruin I have been, shall at length be paid.

senses.d: The state or condition of owing something to another.
ex: I am in your debt.
We owe them a debt of gratitude for taking care of our pets.

senses.d: Money that one person or entity owes or is required to pay to another, generally as a result of a loan or other financial transaction.
ex: Bolsheviki had repudiated the four-billion-dollar debt which the government of the Tsar had contracted with the bankers.
I don't own any stocks or bonds. All my money is tied up in debt.

senses.d: An action at law to recover a certain specified sum of money alleged to be due

ety.text: From Middle English debaten, from Old French debatre (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic desbattere, from Latin dis- (“apart, in different directions”) + battuō (“to beat, to fence”).
From Middle English debat, borrowed from Old French debat, deverbal of debatre, see Etymology 1 for more.

senses.d: To participate in a debate; to dispute, argue, especially in a public arena.
ex: "Debate me, coward!" snarled the completely normal intellectual.

senses.d: To engage in combat for; to strive for.

senses.d: An argument, or discussion, usually in an ordered or formal setting, often with more than two people, generally ending with a vote or other decision.
ex: After a four-hour debate, the committee voted to table the motion.

senses.d: An informal and spirited but generally civil discussion of opposing views.
ex: The debate over the age of the universe is thousands of years old.
There was a bit of a debate over who should pay for the damaged fence.

senses.d: Discussion of opposing views.
